collection.description: At the edge of the village is a flat grey stone covered in names, carved by every generation since the first huts were built.

ask.text:
At the edge of the village is a flat grey stone covered in names, carved by every generation since the first huts were built. Once a year, at the full moon, anyone who wants to may scratch out their name and carve a new one. Most people never do. Some do it once in a lifetime.
(Name) has been staring at (his/her) carved name for an hour. (He/She) has never really liked it. It was (his/her) great-uncle's name, and (his/her) great-uncle was by all accounts a very loud man who fell out of trees.
The carving knife is in (his/her) hand. What should (name) do?

c1o1.text: "(renamed)," says a small voice behind (him/her). It's one of the children, who has been watching the whole time. "Like the brave one in the old stories." (Name) thinks about it, and finds (he/she) likes it very much. (He/She) carves it in big, clear letters. The village gets it wrong for a month, and then never again.

c1o2.text: In the end, (name) just carves the first name that comes into (his/her) head, and steps back, and looks at it. It's an ordinary sort of name. It's nobody's great-uncle's. "That'll do," (he/she) says, and goes home feeling lighter than (he/she) has in years. (He/She) answers to it from the first day, as if it had always been waiting.

c1.text: (Name) scratches out the old name with three careful strokes. Then (he/she) stands there with the knife over the empty stone, and realises (he/she) has no idea what to carve...

c2o1.text: Sitting there, (name) remembers that (he/she), too, has always loved climbing trees, and has fallen out of quite a few. For the first time (he/she) wonders whether (he/she) took up climbing just because of the name. By the end of the night (he/she) has decided (he/she) doesn't need to be anything like (his/her) great-uncle. (He/She) keeps the name, and gives up climbing, and (his/her) knees thank (him/her).

c2o2.text: An elder sits down beside (him/her). "Your great-uncle," says the elder, "was loud because he was always laughing. He fell out of trees because he climbed up to fetch the children's lost balls. He was the kindest man I ever knew." (Name) looks at the carving for a long time. Then (he/she) picks up the knife and carves it deeper.

c2.text: (Name) puts the knife down. (He/She) runs (his/her) fingers over the old carving, worn smooth at the edges, and sits by the stone until the moon is high...
